clips.text: Here are four sticks, joined at the corners by hinges. Push the top, and the square wobbles into a rhombus. Every stick keeps its length, yet the shape changes.
Now try three sticks. However hard you push, the triangle keeps its shape.
A shape that can't wobble, except by sliding or turning as a whole, is called rigid. That's why bridges and cranes are full of triangles.
Now go to three dimensions: a box of twelve sticks, with six faces. The rules: sticks keep their lengths, and faces stay flat. But a face may change shape.
The box still wobbles. It leans over, and each square face becomes a flat rhombus.
Now meet the truncated dodecahedron: sixty corners, ninety sticks, twenty triangles, and twelve ten-sided faces called decagons.
The triangles can't change shape. But each decagon is a ring of ten sticks that could flex within its plane. Can the whole solid wobble? Pause and make a guess.
In twenty twenty-six, three mathematicians tested thirty-one famous solids this way. This was the only one they couldn't decide. The answer is no. Let's see why.
A first idea: count. In the flat square, each corner needs two numbers, so eight numbers. The sticks give four rules. And sliding or turning the whole square uses three freedoms.
Eight minus four minus three leaves one: exactly the wobble we saw. For the triangle, six minus three minus three leaves zero. Rigid.
In space, each corner needs three numbers, and so does each face's flat plane. That's two hundred and seventy-six numbers.
There are ninety stick rules, and a hundred and eighty rules saying a corner lies on a face. Take away six ways to slide and turn, and zero is left.
But the box also counts to zero, and the box wobbles: some rules quietly repeat each other. Euler's formula makes this count zero for every solid of this kind. Counting can never decide.
To look closer, imagine a wobble just starting. At that first instant, each corner sets off in some direction, at some speed. Draw that as an arrow.
For a stick not to stretch or squash at first, its two ends must move equally along the stick. So the shadows of their arrows on the stick must match.
In the square, the top corners slide sideways and the bottom ones stay put. The upright sticks see two zero shadows; the top stick sees two equal ones. All pass.
An arrow pattern that keeps every length unchanged at the first instant is called an infinitesimal flex. Looking for one is the first-order test.
But passing that test isn't enough. Fix two sticks in a straight line, pinned at both ends, and push the middle joint sideways.
The arrow points straight across both sticks, so both shadows are zero. The first-order test is passed. Yet the joint is stuck.
Move the joint up by a small amount, t. By Pythagoras, each stick would need length the square root of one plus t squared. That's too long, by about half of t squared.

That error grows like t squared, too slowly for the first-order test to see. Could nudging the joint along the line fix it? The left stick needs a nudge left, the right stick a nudge right. Impossible.
That clash is called a second-order obstruction. So the tests come in layers: errors like t, then t squared, then t cubed, and so on.
Now test our solid. The first-order test finds four independent infinitesimal flexes, not counting slides and turns. Here is one of them.
Any mix works too: v zero times the first, plus v one times the second, and so on. Four numbers describe every possible start.
Follow the arrows in a straight line, and the sticks begin to stretch, just as before, by amounts like t squared.
Now the second-order test: bend the path to cancel those t squared errors. Here it always works: all forty second-order numbers are zero. That's where the twenty twenty-six paper had to stop.
The bent path's errors now grow like t cubed. After cancelling all we can, four leftover errors remain, each a cubic in v zero to v three.
A real wobble needs all four leftovers to be zero, for some choice of the four numbers that isn't all zeros. If only all zeros works, no wobble can start.
Here's a small version. Take two numbers, x and y, and two leftovers: x squared minus y squared, and x times y. The first one alone is zero all along these diagonal lines.
The second is zero along the axes. The only point on both is the origin, where x and y are zero.
Algebra proves it. Multiply the first leftover by x, the second by y, and add. The middle terms cancel, leaving x cubed. So if both leftovers are zero, x must be zero.

For the solid, a computer found a certificate, a list of numbers anyone can check, that does the same. It combines the four cubics into v zero to the ninth power, and likewise for v one, v two and v three.
Finding those multipliers takes exact arithmetic. The solid's coordinates involve the golden ratio, about one point six one eight, whose square is itself plus one.
Decimals bring rounding errors, and rounding can fake a wobble. A numerical search in the twenty twenty-six paper found what looked like one. With more careful numerics, it snapped back.
So do the arithmetic on a clock with one thousand and nine hours. One thousand plus twenty lands on eleven. Every answer is exact, and numbers never grow.

On this clock, six hundred and twenty-seven plays the golden ratio. Its square is three hundred and ninety-three thousand, one hundred and twenty-nine, which lands on six hundred and twenty-eight: itself plus one.
And because one thousand and nine is prime, division always works too.
Here is the first leftover, in clock numbers: six hundred and forty-nine v zero cubed, plus nineteen more terms like it.
Each square in this grid stands for one of the two hundred and twenty possible terms whose powers add up to nine. A lit square holds a nonzero number.
Add the first leftover times its multiplier: two hundred and one squares light up. Add the second: one hundred and eighty-two stay lit. The third: one hundred and sixty-one.
And the fourth. Everything cancels except one square: v zero to the ninth, with coefficient exactly one.
The same happens for v one, v two and v three. So if all four leftovers vanish, so do all four numbers: no mix of flexes passes the third-order test.
Terms beyond t cubed only add pieces whose powers add up to ten or more, and a standard result called Nakayama's lemma shows they can't rescue a wobble.
But the real solid lives in the real numbers, not on a clock. Why should the clock's answer count?
Start simple. If a whole number is zero, its clock reading is zero. So a nonzero reading proves the number isn't zero.
A wobble is that kind of zero fact. If the real solid could wobble, its equations, read on the clock, would wobble too. The clock shows no wobble, so the real solid has none.
The reverse fails: one thousand and nine reads zero on its own clock. A clock can invent a wobble, but it can't hide a real one. So one clock is enough.
So what is proved? The truncated dodecahedron is locally rigid: any nearby shape with the same sticks and flat faces is the same solid, moved or turned. It cannot wobble.
It says nothing about far-away shapes that no wobble could reach.
The proof is computer-assisted. A small independent program, using exact arithmetic, rebuilds the solid and its equations from scratch and checks every identity, in under a second.

Turning those identities into rigidity is a written proof. It was reviewed within the project, but not checked step by step by proof-checking software like Lean, and outside experts haven't refereed it yet.
To recap. One: for solids like this, counting always balances, so it can't decide.
Two: four infinitesimal flexes pass the first two layers of tests, but at the third layer, four cubic leftovers rule them all out.
Three: on a clock with one thousand and nine hours, that algebra is exact, and a clock that sees no wobble proves the real solid has none.
Still open: outside experts have yet to check the argument, far-away shapes are untouched, and this settles one solid, not a general rule for which solids need these deeper tests.
